canonical_statement: The review aims to cover the anatomy, microbiology, evaluation, treatment, prevention, and management optimization of odontogenic and orofacial infections.
Odontogenic infections can spread along fascial planes into facial and deep neck spaces and are described as the primary cause of deep neck infection in adults.
Maxillary canine and molar infections can spread into the canine or buccal spaces according to root position relative to muscle insertions.
For mandibular infections, spread medial to roots above the mylohyoid line favors the sublingual space, whereas roots below the line favor the submandibular space.
The oral flora is dominated by aerobes and anaerobes, with Streptococcus prominent; odontogenic infections are generally polymicrobial and are treated broadly even when cultures are available.
Dental caries is identified as the leading cause of odontogenic infection, with periapical abscess described as the most common odontogenic infection.
Definitive dental extraction is presented as the gold-standard source-control treatment for odontogenic or orofacial infection, although selected teeth may be preserved with endodontic therapy.
The review reports that by age 65 more than 90% of people in the United States will have experienced dental caries, and that over 70% of odontogenic infections occur in adults aged 20 to 50 years.
Tobacco use and diabetes are described as the comorbid conditions most commonly associated with odontogenic neck infections.
Patients classically have one to two weeks of worsening dental pain before facial or neck swelling, often with fever, malaise, and decreased oral intake.
Odynophagia, neck or facial pain, trismus, fever, and malaise are common; paresthesia, ocular symptoms, dyspnea, or sialorrhea may occur depending on the site and direction of spread.
Early odontogenic cellulitis can generally be evaluated clinically without imaging when the examination is straightforward.

Point-of-care ultrasound can assess suspected abscess formation; CT with intravenous contrast is an adjunct when ultrasound is limited by bone shadowing or body habitus and can help distinguish cellulitis from abscess.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the face and neck should be considered when complex abscess formation or extension into deep neck spaces is suspected.

Prominent neck or oral swelling with stridor, dyspnea, or respiratory distress requires rapid controlled airway evaluation, preferably with awake flexible laryngoscopy to assess impending obstruction or edema.
For odontogenic cellulitis, the review describes broad-spectrum therapy and lists amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin for patients with penicillin allergy as commonly effective options.
Timely extraction of the necrotic offending tooth is recommended with antimicrobial therapy to remove the infectious nidus and halt progression.
Findings that favor abscess over cellulitis include fluctuance, marked mass effect, and suppurative dental sockets; minor abscesses can often be identified with point-of-care ultrasound without CT.
Abscess drainage is recommended for source control and palliation; transoral drainage has the least morbidity and should be attempted when feasible.

Abscess management may combine needle aspiration, incision and drainage, and temporary drain placement according to size and location, and ultrasound guidance can help confirm the cavity before formal drainage.
An abscess culture swab is recommended, but the review notes that the polymicrobial nature of odontogenic infections means culture results rarely change management.

Patients with extensive odontogenic infection, immunodeficiency, or important medical comorbidity should receive intravenous antibiotics, resuscitation, and inpatient monitoring rather than routine outpatient management.
Ludwig angina is characterized as rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, submental, and sublingual spaces and is an airway emergency.
Respiratory distress, drooling, and a bullfrog appearance of the anterior neck are described as classic findings in Ludwig angina.

Management of Ludwig angina should prioritize airway assessment and stabilization, followed by prompt broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and inpatient admission; surgery may be required for airway control or drainage/debridement.
The review reports that odontogenic sinusitis accounts for nearly 40% of acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis.
Unilateral isolated maxillary sinusitis on imaging is described as a pattern that favors an odontogenic source over typical non-odontogenic rhinosinusitis.

Treatment of odontogenic sinusitis centers on dental or implant source control plus antibiotics, with endoscopic sinus surgery when needed; persistent oroantral fistulas are generally repaired after infection resolution.
Recurrent odontogenic-appearing infection in an otherwise healthy patient, or infection without an obvious dental source, warrants evaluation for malignancy or alternative adjacent sources.

The review summarizes a 200-patient emergency-department cohort in which more than half were discharged the same day with medical therapy, fewer than half were admitted, and approximately half of admitted patients required surgery; one morbidity and two necrotizing soft-tissue infections were reported.
Deep-space spread can extend into parapharyngeal, retropharyngeal, carotid, and prevertebral spaces, with the prevertebral space providing a pathway to mediastinitis or empyema.
Delayed treatment, poor nutrition, poor oral hygiene, and tobacco use are described as factors promoting chronic jaw osteomyelitis.
Chronic odontogenic osteomyelitis is evaluated with CT for sequestration, osteolysis, or necrosis and is treated with prolonged culture-directed antibiotics plus debridement of necrotic bone.
Airway obstruction may sometimes be temporized with nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal airways, but deep parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal obstruction may not respond to these measures.
When definitive airway control is required, awake fiberoptic intubation is described as safe and effective if the glottis can be visualized; some patients require cricothyrotomy or tracheostomy.
Necrotizing fasciitis arising from odontogenic infection is a surgical emergency requiring rapid airway assessment and surgical debridement.

Prevention is centered on dental hygiene, including regular brushing and flossing and twice-yearly dental visits, with professional plaque removal and prompt treatment of caries as secondary prevention.
The review concludes that many odontogenic infections can be evaluated and managed at the bedside, with point-of-care ultrasound useful for equivocal examinations and abscess guidance.
Contrast-enhanced CT is described as often unnecessary in routine odontogenic infection because of radiation exposure, contrast-related risk, and incidental findings that may trigger costly workup.
